verdict.rationale: The verb 'to prophesy' (propheteuo, Strong's G4395) occurs 28 times across the canon and is applied with explicit female subjects. In Acts 2:17-18 the daughters ('daughters', thygateres, a feminine plural noun) and handmaidens (doulas) 'shall prophesy' (propheteusousin). In Acts 21:9 four daughters are 'prophesying' (propheteuousai, a present participle, that is an '-ing' form, in the nominative plural feminine, the subject-form for female plural). In 1 Corinthians 11:5 a woman 'praying or prophesying' carries two present participles in the nominative singular feminine (proseuchomene, 'praying', and propheteuousa, 'prophesying') that presuppose the act as actually occurring. The Hebrew noun 'prophetess' (nebiah, Strong's H5031) runs through the Law, Prophets, and Writings: Miriam in Exodus 15:20, Deborah in Judges 4:4, Huldah in 2 Kings 22:14 and 2 Chronicles 34:22, and Isaiah's wife in Isaiah 8:3. Anna is called a 'prophetess' (prophetis, Strong's G4398) in Luke 2:36. Women also labor in the gospel: 'to toil' (kopiao, Strong's G2872) is used of Mary, Tryphena, Tryphosa, and Persis in Romans 16:6, 12; 'to strive together' (synathleo, Strong's G4866) appears in Philippians 4:3; and 'to serve' (diakoneo, Strong's G1247) describes the women in Luke 8:3. The restriction lexemes (key word-forms) in 1 Timothy 2:12 attach to 'to teach' (didaskein) paired with 'to exercise authority over' (authentein) 'a man' (andros, in the genitive form, meaning of/over a man), forming an authoritative-teaching act over a man. The verb 'to exercise authority' (authenteo) is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible). Confidence is high because the openness strand is dense and pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible), while the lone contested verb only bounds the upper office edge, not the affirmation.

scripture.force: Citing Joel, Peter says 'your daughters shall prophesy' (hai thygateres hymon propheteusousin). The subject 'the daughters' (hai thygateres) is a feminine plural noun and the verb 'shall prophesy' (propheteusousin) is future active third plural, so prophecy is predicated of women as a Spirit-poured reality of the last days, not a hypothetical. The same clause that names the sons names the daughters, placing female prophecy on the same footing.

The Joel citation continues 'upon my handmaidens' (epi tas doulas mou), a feminine plural object, with the same verb 'they shall prophesy' (propheteusousin). The repetition of the female subject in the second half of the parallel statement removes doubt that women are intended agents of prophecy, not merely recipients of the Spirit.

Philip had 'four daughters, virgins, prophesying' (thygateres tessares parthenoi propheteuousai). The participle 'prophesying' (propheteuousai) is a present active participle, that is an ongoing '-ing' form, in the nominative plural feminine (the subject-form for a group of females), agreeing directly with the four daughters, so the narrative reports actual ongoing female prophetic ministry as an unremarkable fact of the church's life.

Paul writes 'every woman praying or prophesying' (pasa gyne proseuchomene e propheteousa), with two present participles ('-ing' forms) that are nominative singular feminine (the subject-form for one female) and presuppose the activity as already occurring. He regulates only the manner, an uncovered head dishonors her head, and issues no prohibition of the prayer or prophecy itself. The parallel verse 1 Corinthians 11:4 uses the identical participles 'praying' (proseuchomenos) and 'prophesying' (propheteuon) in the masculine for a man, so the grammar treats male and female praying and prophesying as the same kind of act to be ordered, not forbidden.

Anna is called 'prophetess' (prophetis), a feminine noun, who served in the temple and spoke of the child to all awaiting redemption. The noun 'prophetess' (prophetis) designates a recognized prophetic standing for a woman, anchoring the prophesying-women pattern in the Gospel narrative alongside its appearance in Acts and the epistles.

The base text reads 'Priscilla and Aquila' (Priskilla kai Akylas), naming Priscilla first, and the verbs 'they took aside' (proselabonto) and 'they expounded' (exethento) are aorist (a completed past action) middle third plural. The plural makes Priscilla a joint agent who expounded the way of God to Apollos 'more accurately' (akribesteron). The setting is private reception, not assembly proclamation, so a woman participates in instructing a man outside the formal teaching office.

Older women, 'aged women' (presbytidas), are to be 'teachers of what is good' (kalodidaskalous), an adjective in the feminine plural meaning teachers of what is good. The compound directly assigns a teaching function to women, and the term 'teachers of what is good' (kalodidaskalous) appears only here in the canon, a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible), defining a recognized instructional role within the household and woman-to-woman sphere.

The purpose clause 'that they may train the young women' (hina sophronizosin tas neas) has 'to train' or 'to make sensible' (sophronizo) as a present active subjunctive (an ongoing 'so that they may...' form) with 'the young women' (tas neas) as object. The lexical target is woman-to-woman formation in love of husband and children, locating the female teaching activity outside the man-directed authoritative office.

Tryphena, Tryphosa, and Persis are commended with 'to toil' or 'to labor' (kopiao), the same labor verb Paul uses of his own gospel toil. Of the women he writes 'those who labored in the Lord' (tas kopiosas en kyrio), and of Persis 'who labored much' (hetis polla ekopiasen). The vocabulary places named women in genuine gospel labor, not a domestic-only role, broadening the ministry the proposition affirms.

Paul asks help for women, 'who labored together with me in the gospel' (autais aitines en to euangelio synethlesan moi). The verb 'to strive together' (synathleo) is aorist (a completed past action) active third plural with these women as subject, ranking their gospel labor alongside that of Clement and the rest of his co-workers, an explicitly public ministry partnership.

Joanna, Susanna, and many other women, 'who were ministering to them out of their possessions' (aitines diekonoun autois). The verb 'to minister' or 'to serve' (diakoneo) is imperfect (ongoing or repeated past action), marking sustained ministry, and the relative clause makes the women the active subjects of the serving. This grounds the wide-ministry strand of the proposition in the Gospel narrative.

The restriction reads 'but I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man' (didaskein de gynaiki ouk epitrepo oude authentein andros). The two infinitives 'to teach' (didaskein) and 'to exercise authority' (authentein) are joined by 'nor' (oude) and governed by 'a man' (andros) in the genitive (the 'of/over' grammatical form), targeting a teaching act coupled with exercising authority over a man. 'To exercise authority' (authenteo) is a hapax legomenon (a word that occurs only once in the whole canon), so its precise force is lexically thin and contested. The prohibition is specific to this man-directed teaching-with-authority act and does not lexically reach prayer, prophecy, or the female instruction commanded in Titus 2:3-4.

The clause 'the women should be silent in the churches' (hai gynaikes en tais ekklesiais sigatosan) uses 'to be silent' (sigao) with 'it is not permitted them to speak' (ouk epitrepetai autais lalein), and 'let them be submissive' (hypotassesthosan). Read absolutely it would bar all female speech, but the verb 'to speak' (lalein) here is glossed by the very next verse as the speech the women must instead take home, so the silence term is bounded to a specific kind of speaking rather than to prophecy or prayer.

'But if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home' (ei de ti mathein thelousin, en oiko tous idious andras eperotatosan). The conditional (an 'if-then' clause) ties the silenced speech to 'to learn' (manthano) and 'to ask' (eperotao), framing the prohibited 'speaking' (lalein) as in-assembly questioning that should be deferred to the home, not as the prophetic or prayer speech the proposition affirms.

complicating_texts.resolution: The 'to be silent' (sigao) silence command, taken as an absolute, would contradict the proposition and the praying-prophesying woman of 1 Corinthians 11:5. Lexically it is bounded by its own context: verse 35 names the remedy as asking husbands at home about what the women 'wish to learn' (mathein thelousin), so the silenced 'speaking' (lalein) is framed as disruptive in-assembly questioning rather than prophecy or prayer. The wide ministry the proposition affirms, prayer, prophecy, testimony, and woman-to-woman teaching, is not the speech the silence term targets, so the complication bounds rather than negates the practice.

The restriction couples 'to teach' (didaskein) with 'to exercise authority over a man' (authentein andros), naming an authoritative-teaching-over-a-man act, and 'to exercise authority' (authenteo) is a single-occurrence hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) whose exact sense cannot be triangulated from canon usage. The passage limits one specific office function but does not lexically reach prayer, prophecy, testimony, or the 'teachers of what is good' (kalodidaskalous) teaching role of older women in Titus 2:3-4. It therefore constrains the upper boundary of the proposition, the authoritative-teaching office, while leaving the wider ministry activity standing.

variants.note: No variant units were supplied in the bundle and these texts fall outside the open-cbgm 3 John ECM (critical edition of New Testament textual variants) published scope. The well-known transposition of 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 in some witnesses is a placement variant that does not alter the lexical force used here, since the verdict treats that silence clause only as a bounded complicating text. The Acts 18:26 name order, with Priscilla first in the base text, is a known minor variant but does not change the plural-verb shared-agency reading.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the restriction in 1 Timothy 2:12 as limited to the authoritative-teaching-and-authority-over-a-man office, which leaves prayer, prophecy, testimony, and the instruction of women and children explicitly open. The 'teachers of what is good' (kalodidaskalous) role of Titus 2:3, the praying-prophesying woman of 1 Corinthians 11:5, and the prophesying daughters of Acts 2:17-18 and Acts 21:9 confirm a real but bounded non-authoritative ministry.

Notes the same prophecy and labor texts but reads 'to exercise authority' (authenteo) as a narrow, disputed-sense hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) and 1 Corinthians 14:34 as a bounded or text-critically suspect silence, concluding that female ministry is open even more broadly than the proposition states. Either way the narrower claim, that non-authoritative ministry is open, is affirmed, since both lenses grant the prophecy and gospel-labor texts.

hermeneutics.notes: Both frameworks converge in affirming the limited proposition under test, that women may minister outside the authoritative-teaching office. They diverge on the scope of the restricted office itself, which this question does not adjudicate. The convergence is what makes confidence high: the disagreement is about the ceiling, not about whether non-authoritative ministry is open.

stem_audit.notes: The stem describes a set of ministry practices and names an authoritative-teaching office as a boundary category. The core claim, that women pray, sing, prophesy, give testimony, and teach women and children, is directly testable from the lexical pattern and is not framed to presuppose its answer. The phrase outside the authoritative-teaching office names a contested boundary, but the verdict is derived from the speech-act, prophecy, and labor lexemes (key word-forms) themselves, so the stem is treated as neutral. Verdict unchanged from the prior file; confidence raised from medium to high and pan_canonical raised from false to true after direct queries showed the prophesying-women pattern spans the Law, Prophets, Writings, Gospels, Acts, and epistles.

lay_summary: The original-language pattern shows women clearly engaged in several kinds of ministry, and the strongest thread is prophecy. The Greek word for prophesying (propheteuo) occurs twenty-eight times across the canon, and it is applied directly to women: in Acts your daughters (thygateres) and handmaidens (doulas) will prophesy, four daughters of Philip are described as prophesying (propheteuousai) with a feminine participle (an '-ing' form matching a female subject), and in First Corinthians 11 a woman praying or prophesying (proseuchomene, propheteuousa) is spoken of with present participles that take the act as already happening, the very same words used one verse earlier of a man. The Old Testament Hebrew noun for a prophetess (nebiah) names Miriam, Deborah, Huldah, and others, so the pattern runs from the Law through the Prophets and Writings into the Gospels, where Anna is called a prophetess (prophetis), and on into Acts and the letters. Women also labor in the gospel: the same toil word Paul uses of himself (kopiao) is used of Mary, Tryphena, Tryphosa, and Persis, other women labored together with him (synathleo), and women ministered (diakoneo) to Jesus out of their own means. Priscilla, named first in the text, jointly explained the way of God to Apollos in private, and older women are called teachers of what is good (kalodidaskalous) who train the younger women. Set against all this, the limiting text in First Timothy attaches its prohibition to teaching joined with exercising authority over a man (authenteo), and that authority word appears only once in the whole canon, a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible), so its exact force cannot be pinned down. The silence command in First Corinthians 14 reads strongly alone, but its own next verse ties it to questions that should be taken home to husbands, so it bounds a disruptive kind of speech, not prayer or prophecy. The words therefore support a real distinction. Women verifiably pray, prophesy, give testimony, labor in the gospel, and teach women and children, while the restricting texts target one specific authoritative office over men. Confidence is high because the openness is dense and spans the whole canon, and divergence is only about where the upper boundary falls.
